ECE 6390 / Digital signals

I/Q & decisions

From the figure to the physics

Fig. 1 shows how constellation spacing connects spectral efficiency with noise-sensitive decisions.

A passband symbol can be represented as s(t) = I cos ωct − Q sin ωct. Its I/Q point selects amplitude and phase, and an M-point alphabet carries log₂M coded bits per symbol.

At fixed average symbol energy, adding more points generally reduces their separation relative to noise. Under the displayed equal-noise model, a receiver chooses the nearest symbol point.

Symbol errors and bit errors depend on different information. A bit-error calculation also needs the bit labeling, while coding and a complete channel model further affect performance. A fixed displayed noise realization is an illustration rather than an error-rate forecast.

Example

QPSK carries 2 coded bits per symbol, 16-QAM carries 4, and 64-QAM carries 6. Their average-energy normalization must match before comparing spacing.

Model and course sources

    Practice

    1. Why can two different bit labelings of the same constellation have the same symbol-error count but different bit-error counts?

    A wrong destination point can differ from the transmitted label in one or several bits.

    Symbol decisions depend on point geometry, while bit errors depend on how labels differ between those points. The same wrong symbol can flip different numbers of bits under different labelings.
